extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of municipal government and municipal reform (policymakers, civic reformers)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and recommended practices for structuring, administering, and reforming municipal governments in the United States (early 20th-century perspective). Focuses on charters, administrative organization, civil service, finance oversight, and anti-machine measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual fairness in criticism of American cities
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating reproach, take into consideration the general conditions under which the cities have been compelled to work (rapid growth, absence of pre-existing nucleus of wealth, freest use of public credit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The necessity of making great cities quickly out of 'nothing' compelled lavish expenditure under pressure for quick results and exposed cities to extravagance, wastefulness, and dishonesty; critics should weigh these circumstances before judging material failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow time as an element of city development
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is a necessary element in making a great city; American cities are judged by size rather than by the time which has entered into their growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvement in paving and street cleaning over time shows that many material defects are partly due to rapidity of growth, so assessments should account for the stage of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance current needs with investment in permanent plant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid discounting the future so freely in order to secure permanent plant at the cost of providing adequately for current needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American cities have sometimes failed to provide for current life of their population while accumulating permanent plant; once the permanent plant is paid for, cities should focus on current-service improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foresight in preserving open spaces and planning for future growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities should preserve small open parks and generally make room for future growth and beauty through far-sighted provision rather than later tearing down and replacement at great cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of foresight (e.g., failure to reserve open parks) is a common shortcoming; western cities erred less than Atlantic coast cities, but the general pattern of expensive replacement repeats European precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: City charters must grant adequate powers / promote home rule
rubrics_metrics.description: City charters should be legal instruments granting the community authority to act as a corporation with sufficient powers to grow without constant resort to the State legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many American cities grew out of towns and had to go to the legislature for charters and additional powers, reform aims to enable cities to make their own charters (charter-making/home-rule) and reduce legislative interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit legislative interference with municipal details
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent the State legislature from interfering in the details of city expenditure and administration; require notice to local authorities before laws affecting a city are passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: New York amendment (1894) requires submission of bills affecting a city to local authorities and gives the city a chance to accept or reject; constitutional amendments in many States have aimed at this limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable city-made charters (charter autonomy) with limited legislative amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant cities the authority to make their own charters which are not easily amendable by the State legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States such as Missouri, California, Washington, Minnesota, Colorado (and later Oregon, Oklahoma, Michigan) provided mechanisms for city charters; in California city charters must be confirmed by the legislature but have been routinely affirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency of tenure and Civil Service Reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanency of tenure for subordinate administrative officials and the adoption of civil service principles are essential to securing efficient city administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the U.S. adoption of Civil Service Reform (1883), States and cities have applied merit systems; permanence reduces instability caused by patronage and improves administrative competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate executive appointment and removal power for responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate the power to appoint and remove administrative department heads in the mayor to secure responsibility and effective administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large cities (e.g., New York, Philadelphia, Boston under new charter) have given the mayor absolute appointment/removal power; this centralization is seen as a means to make elected leadership accountable for administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit-based appointments: appoint recognized experts and require civil-service certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments to responsible offices should be of 'recognized experts' or persons specially fitted by education, training, and experience, and be made without regard to party or residence, subject to civil service certification of fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston's charter requires the mayor to appoint experts 'without regard to party affiliation or residence' and makes appointments operative only if a majority of the State Civil Service Commission certifies qualifications within thirty days; this gives the State administrative, not legislative, control focused on fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent Finance Commission for publicity and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a permanent finance commission with authority to investigate, publish, and advise to secure full publicity of municipal finance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boston's Finance Commission (five members appointed by the Governor) is intended to provide public oversight of finance; the Commission's recommendations reflect a trend toward institutionalized financial accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boston Finance Commission's recommended reforms (summarized)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of legislative measures judged essential for redeeming municipal government: simplified ballot; abolition of party nominations; a single small at-large city council; concentration of executive power in the mayor; administration by trained experts; and full publicity via a permanent finance commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission's six-point program is presented as an 'intelligent effort to find a remedy for a widespread evil'; these measures together aim to simplify elections, reduce partisan machine control, centralize executive responsibility, professionalize administration, and secure transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission (Galveston) plan for combined legislative-administrative government
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the 'Commission' or 'Galveston' plan: a small governing board (e.g., five members) with combined legislative and administrative powers, presided over by a Mayor-President, dividing administration of departments among board members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originated in Galveston after the 1900 tidal wave emergency; worked well in moderate-sized cities (e.g., Galveston ~37,000 inhabitants) and has been enabled by statute or charter in several States; often more suitable for moderate-size municipalities than for very large cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce number of elective officers; give elected officials ample authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer elective officers with longer terms and ample authority maintain responsibility and efficiency better than numerous short-term elective offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boston's 1909 charter reduced elected officials from 97 to 10; the text argues that responsibility to the people is best maintained when elective officers are few but have adequate power to do right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the spoils system and professionalize politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the demoralizing maxim 'To the Victors belong the Spoils' by curbing patronage and professionalizing the civil service and political machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spoils system made subordinate civil service unstable; civil service reform and permanency of tenure are antidotes to patronage-driven inefficiency and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaken political machines and 'boss' control by encouraging local independence and electoral reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage a body of voters who will not vote solely on national-party lines and adopt reforms (direct primaries, initiative, referendum, recall) to weaken machine control and enable home rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large concentrated populations require organization to 'get out the vote' and that organization can become a dominant 'boss'; reforms that promote local independent voting and direct participation reduce machine power and strengthen municipal self-government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide free public cultural and educational institutions integrated with schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipalities should develop free cultural institutions (natural history museums, art museums, botanical gardens, zoos, aquaria) related to the public school system and serving both scientific usefulness and public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York City's municipal institutions are cited as examples: free, visited by millions, related to public schools, and embodying both public service and scientific usefulness; such amenities are part of a city's civic responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize fiscal scale and ensure transparency and checks on municipal budgets and bond issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that city budgets and bond issuances can vastly exceed state fiscal operations, creating strong pecuniary motives for control of city expenditure; therefore implement transparency, oversight, and finance-control mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York City's 1908 budget and bond issues greatly exceeded those of the State; this creates temptations and opportunities for professional politicians—hence the need for permanent finance commissions and constitutional/charter safeguards.
